presentingComplaint: Brought to ED after a high-speed motorcycle collision with abdominal pain, dizziness and near-collapse
history: Healthy 34-year-old man, unrestrained motorcyclist, thrown against handlebars ~40 minutes ago. Progressive diffuse abdominal pain, light-headedness on sitting up, cold clammy skin and one episode of syncope at the scene. No known bleeding disorder, on no anticoagulants. Paramedics gave 500 mL crystalloid en route with transient improvement. No head injury, no chest pain, no external major haemorrhage seen.
examination: Anxious, pale, cool peripheries with prolonged capillary refill (>3 s) and thready peripheral pulses. Abdomen distended with generalised guarding and rebound, maximal in the left upper quadrant; seat-belt/handlebar bruising over epigastrium. Pertinent negatives: no external exsanguinating wound, no long-bone deformity, chest clear with equal air entry, no raised JVP, no focal neuro deficit.
imaging: FAST scan positive with free fluid in the splenorenal recess and pelvis; portable CXR and pelvic film clear. Contrast CT (after initial stabilisation) shows grade IV splenic laceration with active contrast extravasation and moderate haemoperitoneum.
differentialDiagnoses: Haemorrhagic shock from blunt splenic injury
finalDiagnosis: Hypovolemic (haemorrhagic) shock due to grade IV blunt splenic injury
citations: Harrison 22e - Approach to the Patient with Shock
contraindications: Avoid large-volume crystalloid resuscitation which worsens dilutional coagulopathy and rebleeding - use balanced 1:1:1 blood product transfusion and permissive hypotension until surgical control
Vasopressors are not a substitute for volume/haemorrhage control and may mask ongoing bleeding
edgeCases: Young fit patients maintain SBP by intense vasoconstriction and may look deceptively stable until ~30% blood loss (class III) then decompensate abruptly
Beta-blocker use or athletic conditioning can blunt the compensatory tachycardia and mask the degree of blood loss
expectedMaiK: The tachycardia, narrow pulse pressure, cool clammy peripheries, rising lactate and a positive FAST after blunt trauma indicate haemorrhagic (hypovolemic) shock from intra-abdominal bleeding. Prioritise haemorrhage control with activated major-haemorrhage protocol and balanced blood products, not crystalloid, alongside urgent surgical/IR intervention.
expectedNextQuestions: Is there ongoing external or occult blood loss and what is the estimated volume?
Any anticoagulant/antiplatelet use or known coagulopathy?
expectedInvestigations: Contrast CT abdomen/pelvis (trauma protocol) once transiently stabilised
Coagulation profile / point-of-care viscoelastic testing and group-and-crossmatch
